title: Projectify - JavaScript + D3.js Single Page Application
blurb: Rough order of magnitude estimate single page web application for Medical Office Fit-outs
label: WEB DEVELOPMENT
detail: A data visualization tool that helps commercial building owners and prospective tenants forecast tenant fit-out costs at the concept stage, before design documents are available. Users input square footage and select a construction type to generate rough-order-of-magnitude (ROM) projections driven by $/SF benchmarks compiled from completed medical office fit-outs. Results render on an interactive D3.js bar chart that supports real-time scope adjustment, giving stakeholders immediate visibility into cost drivers and value-engineering opportunities. The tool applies core project controls principles — historical benchmarking, parametric estimating, and visual reporting — to early-stage feasibility decisions where cost certainty is lowest and the impact of scope choices is highest.

objectives.body: Compile $/SF benchmarks from completed medical-office fit-outs and expose them as live inputs so feasibility-stage estimates respond to scope changes in real time.
Render the ROM as an interactive bar chart where scope dials drive the chart directly, surfacing the dominant cost drivers without requiring spreadsheet literacy.
Build the app as a vanilla SPA (JavaScript + D3) rather than React, to learn the underlying state and rendering primitives that frameworks abstract away.

objectives.lead: Project controls principles for early-stage estimating
objectives.body: Apply historical benchmarking, parametric estimating, and visual reporting at the feasibility stage where cost certainty is lowest and scope decisions have the highest leverage.

challenges.body: Detailed notes on D3.js scale handling, benchmark normalization across mixed-source fit-outs, and SPA state management without a framework are not yet documented here.

futureFeatures.body: Projectify was built as a learning exercise rather than a maintained product; no formal roadmap exists. Likely directions if revisited: expanded fit-out type library (lab, classroom, retail), confidence-interval bands on the ROM, and exportable estimate summaries.

title: Weave - Full Stack Web Development
blurb: A travel planning tool built to demonstrate the ability to deploy a full-stack application. Additional features include the integration of google maps API and nodemailer.
label: WEB DEVELOPMENT
detail: Weave is a MERN-stack group trip planning app developed and launched in one week. It pairs a Node + Express backend with a MongoDB NoSQL database. Users search businesses and points of interest via Google Places autocomplete and pin them onto an interactive map, building a shared itinerary across the group.
description: Weave is a MERN-stack group trip planning app developed and launched in one week. It pairs a Node + Express backend with a MongoDB NoSQL database. Users search businesses and points of interest via Google Places autocomplete and pin them onto an interactive map, building a shared itinerary across the group.

objectives.body: Ship a working MERN app — frontend, API, database, and hosting — end-to-end in a single sprint, prioritizing deploy-readiness over feature breadth.
Wire Google Places (autocomplete + map rendering) and Nodemailer into a single coherent UX where search, pin, and notify all feed the same itinerary state.
Use React-Redux to keep the shared itinerary in sync across multiple users' views without round-tripping through the backend on every interaction.

objectives.lead: NoSQL document modeling for trip data
objectives.body: Model trips, members, and pinned POIs as nested documents in MongoDB rather than relational tables, leaning on the document model for the natural shape of itinerary data.

challenges.body: Sprint-specific challenges (deployment quirks, API quota handling, real-time itinerary sync edge cases) are not yet documented here. The project was built in a one-week sprint and challenges were resolved on the fly without a retrospective.

futureFeatures.body: Weave was built as a learning sprint rather than an ongoing product; no feature roadmap has been defined. Likely directions if revisited: persistent user accounts, mobile-responsive itinerary view, and an export-to-calendar flow.

title: Power BI - Agency Contingent Employee Staffing Tracker
blurb: A reporting tool built to manage a contingent staffing program placing personnel into agency roles.
label: DASHBOARD
detail: A Power BI reporting tool for a contingent staffing program. It tracks candidates from application through placement and surfaces hiring pipeline, interview scoring, and margin on each placement. The model is four tables — roles, candidates, interviews, and status history — with Excel kept as the data entry layer so all calculations stay in Power BI. The headline ranking metric was reworked late in the build from interview score to gross margin per placement, which forced modeling of bill rate against pay rate.
description: A Power BI reporting tool for a contingent staffing program. It tracks candidates from application through placement and surfaces hiring pipeline, interview scoring, and margin on each placement. The model is four tables — roles, candidates, interviews, and status history — with Excel kept as the data entry layer so all calculations stay in Power BI. The headline ranking metric was reworked late in the build from interview score to gross margin per placement, which forced modeling of bill rate against pay rate.

objectives.lead: Four-table relational model in Power BI
objectives.body: Keep roles, candidates, interviews, and status history as separate fact/dim tables joined on stable keys, with Excel as the edit layer and DAX as the calculation layer.

objectives.lead: Sort-order columns in Power Query, not DAX
objectives.body: Build numeric sort keys for pipeline stage as Power Query conditional columns so they're computed before the data model loads, sidestepping DAX calculated-column circular dependencies.
Pull role fields through each candidate's own role ID (not directly from the Roles table) and lock the Candidates→Interviews relationship to a single direction to prevent fan-out.
Model bill rate against pay rate so the placement ranking reflects gross margin rather than interview score — a more decision-useful metric for the program owner.

challenges.lead: Circular dependency on DAX sort key
challenges.body: Building the pipeline sort key as a DAX calculated column triggered a circular dependency. Resolved by moving the sort key into Power Query as a conditional column, which evaluates before the data model loads.

The candidate table showed each candidate against every role because role fields were being pulled straight from the Roles table and two competing relationship paths existed. Resolved by looking up role fields via each candidate's own role ID and correcting cross-filter direction on Candidates→Interviews.

challenges.lead: Late metric pivot from interview score to gross margin
challenges.body: Switching the ranking metric mid-build meant adding bill rate and pay rate to the model and reworking the headline table — a deliberate exercise in the cost of late metric changes versus locking metrics up front.

futureFeatures.body: The status history table is in the model but not yet visualized; add average cycle time per stage and bottleneck detection to the program-owner view.
Now that gross margin is modeled at the placement level, roll it up by recruiter to support compensation and coaching conversations.

title: Power BI - Risk Register Dashboard
blurb: Construction risk register dashboard built around a Python update pipeline: dated entries written into the source Excel register are parsed and appended to a separate update table that powers the dashboard's trend and history visuals.
label: DASHBOARD
detail: Power BI risk register dashboard for a single-contract bridge and utility relocation project, built on PMBOK qualitative risk screening — a 5×5 probability-impact matrix using P × MAX(C,S) scoring with Low / Medium / High banding. The data architecture separates the register (the human-edit surface) from a Risk_Updates flat table (the time-series source), joined many-to-one on a stable risk_id key. A companion Python script handles append-only propagation — parsing new dated entries from the register's mitigation_log column and appending them as rows to Risk_Updates with year inference via a documented month rule. Power BI refreshes off both files via direct file connections; script appends flow through without manual remodeling. Built with synthetic data designed to exercise every visual, not represent real project record.

objectives.lead: Separation of edit surface and time-series source
objectives.body: Keep the register as the human-friendly edit layer and route history into a separate Risk_Updates flat table joined on a stable risk_id, avoiding the trap of growing a single sheet into both roles.
Parse mitigation_log entries with year inference and append to Risk_Updates without rewriting history; month-rule edge cases are documented in the script.

Implement the 5×5 P × I matrix with P × MAX(C,S) scoring and Low/Medium/High banding such that the matrix renders all 25 cells including empties — which requires a disconnected axis table, not just the data.

objectives.lead: New DAX patterns for trend & heat
objectives.body: Author AVERAGEX with RELATED for the average-score trend across a to-one relationship without invoking bidirectional cross-filter, plus a single P × I cell-score measure shared across cost-impact, schedule-impact, and max-impact matrix variants.

challenges.lead: Forcing matrix cells to render including empties
challenges.body: Default Power BI suppresses zero-count cells, breaking the 5×5 layout. Resolved with a disconnected axis table and a SELECTEDVALUE-driven count measure so every cell paints whether or not risks fall in it.

challenges.lead: Avoiding the bidirectional cross-filter trap on trend
challenges.body: The average-score trend across the to-one Risk_Updates relationship initially called for bidirectional filtering, which would have corrupted unrelated measures. Resolved with AVERAGEX + RELATED to compute through the existing single-direction relationship.

Page 1 visuals all scope to mitigation_status = active, but the resolved-count tile on the same page needed to ignore that filter. Resolved with a CALCULATE override on the count measure rather than splitting the page.

challenges.lead: Year inference on parsed mitigation_log entries
challenges.body: Free-text dated entries in the register lack explicit years; the Python parser uses a documented month rule with edge-case warnings rather than guessing silently.

futureFeatures.body: A revamp of this dashboard using Claude Code and an MCP-driven workflow is a separate project on this site (Risk Register Revamp); it carries forward the data architecture decisions and re-authors the visuals through the PBIR CLI.
Pair the qualitative P × I matrix with quantitative methods (expected value, Monte Carlo on contingency). The current build is qualitative screening only.

title: Power BI - Risk Dashboard Revamp using Claude Code
blurb: Revamp of a Risk Power BI dashboard with Claude Code, driving edits through the Power BI MCP server and visual review through the Chrome MCP server
label: DASHBOARD
detail: Revamp of a risk dashboard that was initially created by a project controls engineer learning the basic mechanical skills of Power BI. The revamped dashboard utilizes an AI-assisted workflow defined by the learning goals below.
description: A dashboard revamp where Claude Code edits the files directly, the Power BI MCP server updates the data model, and the Chrome MCP server lets Claude review the rendered report in the browser.

objectives.body: Use an AI-assisted workflow to create high-quality dashboards following industry-recommended architecture and visual design.

Follow an AI-assisted workflow that reduces token usage and context bloat through phased planning, explicit assignment of subagents to subtasks, and a project-level markdown file that updates and clears context at the end of every phase.
Connect Claude Code to Power BI via MCP server.
Provide Claude Code with the ability to view its own work. Employ Test-Driven Development with user-generated test requirements at the end of each phase of the project.
Document each challenge and breakthrough in a concise summary, recorded on a markdown file for future project use.

Python scripts emulate real-project risk-log updates, appending to Risk_Updates_Master.xlsx and replacing Risk_Register_Master.xlsx source data. appendupdates.py has guardrails that alert the user to edge cases where an update date exceeds 1½ months from the append date; current master copies are date-stamped on the last update and moved to the archive folder.
Display an interactive version of the dashboard inside the modal view of this technical project on my portfolio website.

challenges.body: The current Power BI Desktop release errored when opening .PBIP files with Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.2 or higher installed. Reverting Newtonsoft.Json to 13.0.0 restored PBIP file opening through the desktop app.

Conditional formatting authored via the PBIR CLI did not apply to the visuals. A first attempt restructured the AI-assisted procedure around a helper DAX measure returning the hex code, but the helper measure greyed out as a field choice in the dialog. Final resolution had Claude Code reverse-engineer user-authored fx rules to identify the renderer-engaging shape. The method was applied to every new visual type, with per-visual dependencies (active slot index, selector presence, schema version) recorded in a markdown file to seed a Skill for future Power BI projects.

Claude Code defaulted to user-side verification from the desktop app at every stage gate, which risked version overwrites (user saves after agent edits) and added user friction. The agent was instructed to publish and refresh through Microsoft Fabric CLI in the browser instead, reducing user effort, time per project, and the chance of version-control conflicts.

Turnover files from the original manually-built dashboard carried design intent that was deliberately changed or removed during the revamp's planning phase. A custom Skill was authored that prompts Claude Code to replace irrelevant context in the project's CLAUDE.md, keeping the agent aligned with the revamp's current design decisions.

The drillthrough page's Mitigations visual showed a single concatenated string of updates and dates, reading as a sloppy block. A new measure pulls individual risk updates from Risk_Updates to replace the static-column lookup, sorted latest-first with line breaks between entries.

futureFeatures.body: Add seed data for multiple contracts and enable program-level rollups. Repurposing the existing dashboard requires a project dimension with multiple rows, project slicers on every page, and a careful review of which measures need re-aggregation across projects.

Pair the qualitative P×I matrix with quantitative methods (expected value, Monte Carlo on contingency). The current build is qualitative screening only; the quantitative work will be a separate project.

title: ConBon.app — Project Controls Team Kanban Board
blurb: Internal kanban tool for a 4 to 8 person commercial construction team — estimators, schedulers, analysts, and a commercial manager — that surfaces work assignments, priorities, and blockers across active contracts. Built end-to-end through an AI-assisted, phased workflow on a compressed timeline as a venue to practice phased delivery, token discipline, and TDD at the phase-gate level on a real shipping product, not a prototype.
label: WEB DEVELOPMENT
detail: ConBon (controls + kanban) is an internal kanban tool for a 4 to 8 person commercial construction team of estimators, schedulers, analysts, and a commercial manager. The board lets them assign work, set priorities, surface blockers, and balance workloads across active contracts. The whole project was built through an AI-assisted workflow to build a real shipping product rather than a prototype.
description: ConBon (controls + kanban) is an internal kanban tool for a 4 to 8 person commercial construction team of estimators, schedulers, analysts, and a commercial manager. The board lets them assign work, set priorities, surface blockers, and balance workloads across active contracts. The whole project was built through an AI-assisted workflow on a compressed timeline as a venue to practice phased delivery, token discipline, and TDD at the phase-gate level on a real shipping product rather than a prototype.

objectives.lead: AI-assisted delivery on a shipping timeline
objectives.body: Use Claude Code to ship a fully-deployed multi-user web app, not a prototype, in a short calendar window without compromising engineering quality.

Break the build into 14 numbered phases (data model, tRPC, design system, board, mutations, auth, real-time, admin, audit, preferences, Docker, CI/CD, tests) with explicit 'Done when' criteria and one PR per phase.

Maintain a project-level CLAUDE.md as the single source of truth for stack decisions, locked architectural choices, and current status. Refresh it at every phase boundary so future sessions skip rediscovery and stay aligned with current design rather than history.

Each phase merges only after the agent demonstrates the feature against real seed data. Phase 14 formalizes this with a Playwright suite (Chromium, storage-state cookie reuse) and axe-core a11y enforcement that fails CI on any serious or critical WCAG 2.1 AA violation, which is strictly stronger than a Lighthouse score threshold.

Pair familiar React 19 and Next 16 with first-time uses of @dnd-kit for keyboard-accessible drag, tRPC v11 with SuperJSON for end-to-end typing without a manual API layer, Prisma 7's driver-adapter that removes the alpine/musl binary engine dance, Auth.js v5 with JWT sessions, Radix primitives (Dialog, ContextMenu, DropdownMenu, Toast), and Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY into SSE for real-time sync without a separate broker.

Ship to a registered domain (conbon.app) on a real DigitalOcean VPS with Docker multi-stage, Caddy with Let's Encrypt, nightly pg_dump, and GitHub Actions into GHCR with SSH deploys via appleboy/ssh-action. The operational story is part of the build, not bolted on at the end.

challenges.lead: React 19 effect-ordering trap in the preferences provider
challenges.body: The first design split persistence between a root-level ThemeProvider and an (app)-scoped reconciler that wrote DB values upward on mount. The write-back effect fired with stale render-1 closure state and queued a default-value POST that overwrote the actual DB row. Resolution unified ownership into a single PreferencesProvider at root, with the state initializer seeded directly from server-fetched prefs and lastSyncedRef initialized to the same value so the first render is automatically a no-op even under StrictMode.

Prisma 7's CLI eagerly resolves env('DATABASE_URL') in prisma.config.ts on every invocation, breaking a second prisma generate step in the builder stage. Resolution moved generation entirely into the deps stage, before prisma.config.ts is copied into the image, and trusted the carried-forward .prisma/client through subsequent stages. A dummy build-time DATABASE_URL satisfies lib/db.ts's eager validation.

A site-level encode zstd gzip was compressing Server-Sent Event chunks, buffering them inside the encoder until flush and silently defeating real-time delivery in production. Resolution scoped encode to a catch-all handle block and let a separate @sse path /api/events matcher run reverse_proxy with flush_interval -1 and no encoder wrapping the response.

The CardEditModal's date input read with local-timezone accessors and wrote with a local-timezone constructor, so saving a card near midnight UTC produced phantom 'May 21 to May 20' audit diffs on every save. Resolution anchored both directions to UTC (getUTC* on read, Date.UTC(...) on write). The proper schema-level fix of storing dates as string was scoped to a later migration.

The Prisma pool rotates connections and silently drops a registered LISTEN, so naively reusing it for real-time fanout would lose subscriptions on the next pool rotation. Resolution opened a dedicated pg.Client pinned on globalThis so Next dev hot reload doesn't multiply the connection, held the subscription there, and kept the NOTIFY payload tiny at {type, op, id} to stay well under Postgres's 8000-byte atomic limit. Clients pick an invalidation target from the payload and refetch the authoritative list via existing tRPC queries.

CLAUDE.md grew faster than it was curated, and prior-phase decisions sometimes conflicted with the current implementation by the time a later phase opened. Resolution wired a /refresh-claude-md skill that consolidates project memory at phase boundaries, locking in new decisions and pruning superseded ones so the next session opens against current state rather than rediscovering it.

futureFeatures.body: The code pipeline is green through Phase 14 and the VPS is provisioned, but the four DEPLOY_* GitHub secrets and the DOMAIN repo variable aren't populated yet, so deploy.yml's deploy job is expected-red on every push to main. Closing this gap turns red into a real regression signal and removes the manual SSH step from the deploy loop.

The current board is a qualitative tool where dragging a card claims it and dragging it back surfaces a blocker. A future pass would mine the AuditLog (already accumulating per-mutation history) for cycle-time per assignee, blocker dwell time, and contract-level throughput, so the commercial manager can spot where work is stuck without reading every card.

title: PMIS Parser - Oracle Email Config → Excel Automation
blurb: Python service that watches an Outlook inbox for Oracle Primavera Unifier submittal notifications, extracts structured data with Claude + Pydantic, and appends each event to a per-project Excel workbook on OneDrive — replacing manual log entry. Microsoft Graph on both ends; ships personal-tenant today, swaps to enterprise M365/SharePoint via config tomorrow.
label: AUTOMATION
detail: An AI-assisted automation that eliminates manual data entry from construction PMIS notification emails. The first vendor target is Oracle Primavera Unifier — chosen because its custom email templates are admin-configured via uDesigner, so the parser's expected shape and the PMIS template are co-designed up front rather than chasing fixed-format drift. The architecture is vendor-agnostic for v2 expansion to Procore, Kahua, and Newforma. Office engineers currently spend a meaningful share of every workday transcribing submittal notifications, workflow step assignments, and review actions from Unifier into an Excel log. This tool reads the email directly from Outlook via Microsoft Graph, extracts the structured update with Claude under a strict JSON schema, and appends the row to the existing project log — all within the 5-minute polling interval. Business impact: redirects roughly one office engineer's worth of mindless transcription per project onto field inspection work, cutting the employer's separate-inspector hiring need while giving the engineer actual construction-site knowledge that automation cannot replace.

objectives.body: Use a phased Plan → Question → Execute → Reflect loop with Q&A interrogation against the original scope doc, ADR-style decision logging, and per-phase handoff documents.
Push depth into per-phase and per-decision markdown files; keep CLAUDE.md a thin index. Each phase's skill list is explicit, and only those skills load at phase start.

Single integration surface for both Outlook mail read and Excel workbook write, replacing the original scope doc's third-party inbound-email vendor and removing the need for per-user forwarding addresses.

Claude with a strict Pydantic-derived JSON schema; prompt caching for the schema/instructions block; confidence scoring with a 'Needs review' flag on low-confidence outputs so the office engineer reviews exceptions, not every row.

v1 ships against personal Outlook.com + OneDrive personal; v2 swaps to enterprise Microsoft 365 + SharePoint with a config-only change, no business-logic rewrite. The same code proves itself in personal demo and production tenant.
Per-phase fixture tests against real captured Unifier notification emails; integration tests against live Graph; end-to-end verification with the verify skill before each phase closes.

challenges.lead: Claude Console API costs for agents to parse emails
challenges.body: LLM extraction is the pipeline's only metered cost, so the design treated tokens as a budget to engineer against. A regex pre-filter on sender and subject ensures Claude runs only on genuine submittal notifications — never on every email in the inbox. I benchmarked accuracy against cost across Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus and settled on Haiku, then cached the ~3,600-token instruction prompt so repeat calls hit cache, reaching an ~87% cache-hit ratio in practice. Per-email cost lands around a cent — comfortably under the $20/month ceiling the tool enforces and reports on.

Power BI Pro alone does not include Exchange Online or SharePoint Online, so the user's own M365 tenant did not expose a usable mailbox. Fix: build v1 against an Outlook.com personal mailbox and OneDrive personal, using Graph endpoint paths identical to enterprise M365 except for the MSAL authority string. The v2 swap to a real tenant is approximately ten lines of config.

Outbound calls to api.anthropic.com from the corporate network would require IT approval — a process outside the user's control and outside the build timeline. Fix: v1 runs on the user's personal workstation; portability across tenants and networks means production adoption inside the company can happen later without a rewrite.

challenges.lead: Regex-per-vendor cost calculus inverted at personal scale
challenges.body: The scope doc front-loaded per-vendor regex parsers with LLM as a fallback — a model that makes sense at high volume but inverts at single-mailbox scale, where engineering cost dominates API spend. Fix: LLM-first with strict Pydantic validation; regex shortcuts deferred to v2 as a cost optimization, not a v1 architectural commitment.

challenges.lead: Multi-party submittal workflow vs. single-status column
challenges.body: Construction submittal workflows pass between designer, CM, GC, and DOR with distinct dates per handoff. A naive 'current status + status date' schema would lose the timeline that document-controls practice requires. Fix: per-event date columns updated in place on a Submittals sheet (designer-assigned, designer-reviewed, CM-assigned, GC-review, DOR-review), plus a separate History sheet capturing every notification ever processed as an append-only audit trail.

futureFeatures.body: Move from personal Outlook.com + OneDrive personal to a company M365 tenant + SharePoint team site. Designed as a config-only swap; same MailSource and OutputSink interfaces, different MSAL authority and workbook handle.

Add RFINotification and ChangeOrderNotification schemas alongside the existing SubmittalNotification; route each entity type to its own sheet within the per-project workbook. v1's schema versioning and entity-typed writer routing accept this without breaking existing data.

futureFeatures.lead: SharePoint folder walk + PDF submittal enrichment
futureFeatures.body: Beyond the email body, traverse the project's Submittals/ folder tree to locate the actual submittal PDF; use Claude's native PDF support to extract description, comments, and contractor notes the email summary omits — producing a single richer log row per submittal instead of relying on whatever the notification template happened to include.

title: Power BI - Construction Dashboards Capstone
blurb: Multi-page Power BI report for a Sound Transit roadway bridge program — a new vehicular concrete bridge and an adjacent earthwork package, modeled as two fully-independent contracts. Schema anchored to CSI MasterFormat 2020, CSI 01 33 00 submittal types, and PMIS workflow statuses so the same model hosts any contract type without schema changes. Authored entirely in PBIR/TMDL via Claude Code paired with the Fabric CLI and Power BI Modeling MCP, with self-verification through Tabular Editor BPA, a DAX-UNION smoke harness, and UIAutomation-driven Desktop screenshots.
label: CAPSTONE
detail: Personal capstone closing out a Power BI and reporting learning track for a project controls engineer in commercial construction. The build is a multi-page Power BI report for a Sound Transit roadway bridge program — a new vehicular concrete bridge and an adjacent earthwork package, modeled as two fully-independent contracts — with a semantic model anchored to CSI MasterFormat 2020, CSI 01 33 00 submittal types, and PMIS-standard workflow statuses so the same model serves any project type without schema changes. Authored entirely in the text-based PBIR/TMDL format and driven by Claude Code paired with the Fabric CLI and the Power BI Modeling MCP, with self-verification through Tabular Editor's Best Practice Analyzer, a DAX-UNION smoke harness, and UIAutomation-driven Desktop screenshots.
description: Personal capstone closing out a Power BI and reporting learning track for a project controls engineer in commercial construction. The build is a multi-page Power BI report for a Sound Transit roadway bridge program — a new vehicular concrete bridge and an adjacent earthwork package, modeled as two fully-independent contracts — with a semantic model anchored to CSI MasterFormat 2020, CSI 01 33 00 submittal types, and PMIS-standard workflow statuses so the same model serves any project type without schema changes. Authored entirely in the text-based PBIR/TMDL format and driven by Claude Code paired with the Fabric CLI and the Power BI Modeling MCP, with self-verification through Tabular Editor's Best Practice Analyzer, a DAX-UNION smoke harness, and UIAutomation-driven Desktop screenshots.

objectives.body: Anchor every fact and dimension (Risk, RFI, Submittal, ChangeOrder, CostLine, CommissioningItem, Schedule) to industry standards — CSI MasterFormat 2020 cost coding, CSI 01 33 00 submittal types, PMIS workflow statuses, configurable per-project disciplines — so the same model can host a bridge contract, an earthwork contract, or an elevator/escalator replacement without code changes. Data drives the differences, not the model.

Build the entire report — 98 measures, 52 relationships (39 active + 13 inactive), five pages of native and Deneb Vega-Lite visuals, a multi-bookmark Cost & Performance page with a custom waterfall and an SOV detail table — directly in TMDL and PBIR JSON via the Fabric CLI and the powerbi-modeling MCP. Desktop is only used for reload and screenshot, never for authoring.

Drive measure design, relationship topology, calculation groups, and DAX refactoring through Claude Code with the Power BI Modeling MCP. The agent owns the loop: author TMDL, refresh the model, run smoke and BPA, screenshot Desktop, compare against the expected-values table for the page, iterate.

Give Claude Code the ability to verify its own work end-to-end: pbir validate for schema, Tabular Editor 2 BPA for model hygiene, a generated DAX-UNION smoke query that evaluates every measure under All / Pkg4 / Pkg6 filter contexts, a relationship-ambiguity detector, and a UIAutomation Desktop driver that reloads the file and dismisses modals so screenshots can be taken without a human in the loop. The user reviews finished pages, not partial fixes.

objectives.lead: Phased workflow with hard plan-lock gates
objectives.body: Run the build under a phased-workflow skill with explicit plan-lock gates, one atomic ADR per locked decision, and a turnover doc at every phase boundary so the next session starts from a clean, self-contained context. Token discipline: defer reading large source files (real-data Excels, prior project artifacts) until the phase that actually needs them.

Maintain per-phase plan docs (docs/0N_*.md), atomic ADRs per locked decision (docs/decisions/), turnover docs at every phase boundary (docs/artifacts/handoffs/), and a project-specific powerbi-lessons skill that captures generalizable Power BI traps for future builds.

challenges.lead: TMDL whitespace as silent DAX-syntax corruption
challenges.body: Mid-Phase 3 a 16-measure cascade flipped to SYNTAXERROR placeholders after what looked like a clean edit. Root cause: TMDL property lines (formatString, displayFolder) indented to three tabs were parsed as continuation of the DAX expression block above them. No error, no validation failure — just every downstream measure quietly evaluating to error. Auto-fixed with a 35-line bulk dedent. Lifted into the powerbi-lessons skill as a top-of-file gotcha; smoke now runs after every TMDL mutation.

challenges.lead: DAX evaluates clean but the visual renders blank
challenges.body: The native KPI card evaluates its Indicator measure under the TrendLine field's date filter context, so a measure returning a real value via EVALUATE ROW("v", [m]) can still render BLANK on the card. Discovered during the Risk page (single-snapshot fact, no temporal spread → TrendLine cascade collapses the indicator). Codified as a standing rule: every visual fix attempt must close the loop with a Desktop reload and a screenshot compared against the page's expected-values table. DAX query results are necessary but never sufficient — Claude Code self-checks via screenshot before claiming a fix is done.

challenges.lead: Snapshot-table fan-out silently inflating fact counts
challenges.body: The Overview page shipped with activity counts 3× the true value because the schedule fact joined to a snapshot dimension and measures aggregated across Baseline + Update 1 + Update 2 with no latest-snapshot gate. Caught only when the Schedule & Gantt page added a per-snapshot view and the numbers stopped reconciling with Overview KPIs. Fix: added a calculated IsLatestSnapshot flag on the snapshot dim and refactored 8 measures to gate on it; backfilled the lesson as a pattern so every full-replace snapshot table in the model now follows the same shape.

Claude Code consistently inferred 'ready to lock the plan' from a handful of accepted multiple-choice answers and started writing CLAUDE.md, 00_plan.md, and ADRs before the user had actually confirmed the lock. Codified as an explicit gate in the phased-workflow skill: present a recap covering everything that would lock (phase list, stack, cross-cutting concerns, DoD, out-of-scope, ADR titles), prompt explicitly for 'ready to lock?', and write nothing until the user replies. Saved as a reusable feedback memory.

The agent twice retroactively edited locked ADRs based on indirect evidence (a sibling project's wireframe mock data, a tangentially-related README) without the actual source data in hand. Codified the explicit rule: schema decisions require actual source data AND the relevant wireframe before any iteration; locked ADRs that surface a concern stay flagged 'preliminary, pending Phase N validation' rather than getting silently superseded by speculation.

challenges.lead: PBIR JSON paths that fail silently
challenges.body: Several visual properties have look-alike paths that the schema accepts at validate-time but the renderer ignores. Three caught the hard way: slicer orientation lives at objects.general.orientation as an integer, not data.mode = 'HorizontalList' (silent no-op); alt text lives at visualContainerObjects.general[0].properties.altText, not objects.general[0] (different scope, same container name); bookmark-wired action buttons need visualContainerObjects.visualLink[].properties.{type, bookmark}, not a root-level visualLink (validate passes, click does nothing). Each one landed in the powerbi-lessons skill with the wrong path AND the right path side-by-side so the lesson sticks.

futureFeatures.body: Carry the schema, ADRs, and self-verification discipline from the Power BI build into a standalone Next.js + Supabase + D3 web app that renders the same dashboards directly from a team's existing logs — Excel uploads, or a linked OneDrive or SharePoint folder — so users never re-key data they already have. Now shipped as the next entry on this site.

Pair the qualitative 5×5 P × I matrix with quantitative methods (expected value, Monte Carlo on contingency reserves). The current build is qualitative screening only; quantitative analysis is a candidate for a model extension or a separate companion project.

title: d3bi.app — D3.js Dashboard App (V1)
blurb: A set of styled, ready-to-use project-controls dashboard templates a team can run on its own data — upload your existing Excel logs, or link a OneDrive or SharePoint folder, and d3bi renders cost/EVM, schedule, RFI/submittal, risk, and quality boards with no data-entry forms anywhere in the path. The charts are authored from raw D3 math (d3-scale, d3-shape, d3-axis) through React JSX rather than composed from a chart library. Now shipped as a login-gated app in production, validated against two real Sound Transit East Link (2 Line) packages — E130 and E320 — at a 31 March 2021 data date.
label: CAPSTONE
detail: Styled, ready-to-use project-controls dashboard templates that render against a team's own data — upload existing Excel logs, or link a OneDrive or SharePoint folder, and the app parses and loads them into a canonical Postgres model on a daily schedule, with no data-entry forms in the path. The chart layer is hand-authored: React owns the DOM and D3 handles only computation (d3-scale, d3-shape, d3-axis), with no chart library. Six manifest-driven boards — Overview plus cost/EVM, schedule, RFI/submittal, risk, and quality — ship as the first templates, deployed to production behind login and validated against a complete, FK-validated dataset modeled on two real Sound Transit East Link packages (E130 and E320) at a 31 March 2021 data date.
description:
d3bi is a set of styled, ready-to-use project-controls dashboard templates that assemble cost/EVM, schedule, RFI and submittal, risk, and quality views from a team's existing logs — upload your Excel logs, or link a OneDrive or SharePoint folder, with no manual data re-entry. Its chart layer is built from raw D3 math (d3-scale, d3-shape, d3-axis) rendered through React, rather than from a charting library. The name contracts "D3" and "BI." It is the standalone successor to an earlier Power BI capstone, rebuilt to author the visualization layer directly rather than compose existing components.

The application is now shipped. A login-gated V1 is deployed to production: six manifest-driven dashboards — an Overview plus the cost/EVM, schedule, RFI/submittal, risk, and quality domains — render live against real program data that the app pulls from the team's own OneDrive, parses, and loads into a canonical Postgres model on a daily schedule, with no data-entry forms anywhere in the path. Access is gated by Supabase Auth (email and password) with defense-in-depth checks at the edge, in the server layouts, and on every data-writing API route. The early artifacts that scoped the work — a decision record, a wireframe of the core dashboard pages, and a complete, FK-validated seed dataset — have all been carried through into a running product, and the decision record has grown into an atomic ADR log that tracks each production decision against the original plan.

That seed — still the data foundation the dashboards and the ingestion path are validated against — is built from two real Sound Transit East Link (2 Line) packages, presented from the construction manager's perspective, with Sound Transit as the owner and the general contractor as the monitored party. E130 covers the I-90 / Crosslake civil work from Seattle to South Bellevue (CM: Jacobs; GC: Kiewit-Hoffman), with a baseline near $651M and a current approved budget near $689.5M. E320 covers the South Bellevue Station, Garage and Guideway (CM: HDR; GC: Shimmick-Parsons), with an original value near $321M and a current approved budget near $331.6M.

Both files share a single data date of 31 March 2021, so the dataset is a snapshot of the program's controls metrics at that point. The date was chosen because it sits in an informative window for project controls: several conditions that later influenced cost and schedule were already measurable in the data before they appeared in summary reporting. The line opened to riders in March 2026. The framing is educational, intended to study what controls metrics can reveal and when, not to assess the parties involved.

At the data date, E130 reads SPI 0.805 and CPI 0.96, with an earned-value forecast (EAC ~$769.7M) above the current approved budget and a forecast finish roughly nine months past the baseline date; the risk register holds 20 open items (3 Critical, 5 High, 12 Medium). E320 shows a milder profile over the same period (SPI 0.923, CPI 0.93, EAC ~$359.8M), consistent with a package behind its original baseline but recovering. The seed also models a quality domain that most controls reporting omits — 32 inspection lots and 51 nonconformance reports on E130 — whose central measure is the gap between quantity installed and quantity accepted (for the trackway plinths, roughly 95% installed against roughly 25% accepted). These leading indicators tend to move before the corresponding risks or change orders are recorded — the property the case study was built to demonstrate, and the one the shipped quality boards now surface directly.

objectives.body: Charts are built from D3 math rendered through React JSX, with React owning the DOM and D3 handling only computation — no d3-selection, and no chart library. A shared shell handles sizing, theme, axes, tooltips, and accessibility; per-chart code carries only the visual encoding. Ten such charts now run across the six production dashboards on this single pattern.

Dashboards are manifest-driven and assembled from data-agnostic chart components: a chart receives a binding object mapping fields to encodings rather than a fixed data shape, so a report defined once renders against any contract. The visual system is tokenized so themes are configurable, with presets layered across system, organization, and personal scopes. The emphasis is visual customization, not a formula builder.

The views are built from logs a team already maintains, with no data-entry forms — a user uploads their Excel logs or links a OneDrive or SharePoint folder, and the pipeline into a canonical Postgres model and out to dashboards runs in production today.

objectives.lead: Serve multiple project types from one schema
objectives.body: A single canonical model spans different contract types, letting the data drive the differences rather than forking the schema per project — validated across the two East Link packages, and next against a second domain.

objectives.lead: Ground the work in real data
objectives.body: The model and the visuals are validated against a sourced, real-program dataset so every figure foots to a believable controls story rather than smoothed synthetic numbers.

challenges.lead: Reducing manual input against a strict schema
challenges.body: The canonical model is normalized and rigid, while real logs vary by company and region. A three-bucket ingestion model resolved the tension: users supply their real logs as-is (Bucket A); the application supplies all keys, dimensions, mappings, and dates (Bucket B); and one-time setup is proposed by the app and confirmed by the user rather than typed in (Bucket C) — realized as a setup section with per-contract settings and a column→field mapping editor. Header alias resolution is app-managed, and readiness is treated as required columns are a subset of present columns, so extra columns are retained and nothing has to be reshaped to fit.

challenges.lead: Joining logs that use different breakdowns
challenges.body: Teams keep separate logs, so multi-file upload is the primary path and the app consolidates internally. Logs using different structures (CSI cost coding, a schedule WBS, spec-section RFIs) are aligned on a time axis derived from each row's own date columns, rather than forced onto a shared key.

The model was validated against two genuinely different real packages — E130 (heavy-civil, GC/CM delivery) and E320 (station and garage, design-bid-build). Flex points were designed in: optional entities that appear for some project types and not others, a configurable segmentation dimension (stations, phases, or floors depending on the work), and multi-standard classification rather than one forced coding scheme.

challenges.lead: Front-loading only what is expensive to reverse
challenges.body: On Postgres with versioned migrations, additive change is inexpensive, so only fact grain, identity strategy, and scoping columns were locked pre-implementation; everything else evolved through migrations as the build progressed. A per-table reference catalog records each column's downstream usage to keep later changes tractable.

challenges.lead: React and D3 DOM ownership, and accessibility
challenges.body: The React-renders / D3-computes pattern was first proven on a non-trivial chart, then scaled to the full set, with accessibility (labels, keyboard navigation, a data-table fallback, and encodings that do not rely on color alone) built into each chart rather than retrofitted — and held in place by axe-core checks in CI.

futureFeatures.lead: A branded public site and marketing landing
futureFeatures.body: Flip routing so the root serves a public, indexable marketing landing while the application moves fully behind login (request-a-demo and log-in, with no public sign-up yet), under a new site skin kept separate from the existing dashboard tokens.
Add a second prebuilt template — an aviation/airport program — alongside the transit template, exercising a true multi-template index driven by the one canonical schema.

Evolve the column→field mapping into a three-panel drag-and-drop surface for assigning a team's columns to canonical fields, with the existing keyboard/dropdown editor retained as the accessible fallback.

futureFeatures.lead: A custom dashboard builder with private templates
futureFeatures.body: A visual builder that emits a serializable manifest, plus per-user private saved templates — the first per-user-private data, scoped at the application layer ahead of the later move to row-level security.
Broader domain coverage, then multi-user with row-level security and audit, and ultimately a multi-tenant SaaS with self-serve trials.

title: d3bi.app — Dashboard Design Assistant Chatbot (V2)
blurb: debi — an in-app AI assistant that turns a plain-language request into a complete, data-validated dashboard and saves it as a reusable template. It reads what a team's uploaded data actually supports through the readiness loop and emits panels, KPIs, and layout that render live, never fabricating a metric — every number traces to the validated earned-value engine, not to model prose. debi is the centerpiece of d3bi's turn from a single dashboard app into a branded, multi-tenant-ready product workspace: a public marketing front door, a multi-template gallery, a drag-and-drop schema-assignment surface, and a two-skin app shell that re-skins the chrome without disturbing the proven dashboard visuals all land alongside it.
label: CAPSTONE
detail: debi is an in-app AI assistant that builds a complete, data-validated dashboard from a plain-language request and saves it as a private, reusable template. It takes the manifest-driven, data-agnostic chart system from V1 and makes it conversational: a user describes the dashboard they want, debi reads what their uploaded data supports through the readiness loop, and emits panels, KPIs, and layout that render live — never inventing a metric, because every figure traces to the validated earned-value engine. debi ships inside d3bi's reframe into a multi-tenant-ready product workspace — a public marketing front door, a multi-template gallery, a drag-and-drop schema-assignment surface, and a two-skin app shell that re-skins the chrome without disturbing the proven dashboard visuals — and the work is in development now, with the shell and skin seam built and debi, the gallery, the drag-and-drop surface, and the marketing landing following as wireframes and a brand sheet arrive.
description:
V2 makes d3bi's dashboard authoring conversational. debi is an in-app AI assistant that takes a request in plain language, reads what a team's uploaded data actually supports through the readiness loop, and emits a full dashboard — panels, KPIs, layout — that renders live and saves as a private, per-user template. It never fabricates a metric: every number debi shows traces to the same validated earned-value engine the V1 templates run on, not to model prose. Turning the V1 chart/manifest system into something a user authors by talking to it is the defining work of this version.

debi ships inside a larger turn — internally "the reframe" — from a single login-gated dashboard app into a branded, multi-tenant-ready product workspace. Routing flips so the root serves a public, indexable marketing landing while the application moves behind login (request-a-demo and log-in, no public sign-up yet). A multi-template gallery presents the product as a multi-project workspace, with a program/project switcher and a second prebuilt template — aviation — joining the original transit set. A persistent app shell (a site top bar plus a left nav) wraps every in-app screen, and a two-skin token seam lets a new site brand re-skin the chrome without disturbing the proven dashboard visual system: the shell reads its own --shell-* tokens, which alias the existing dashboard tokens until a brand sheet lands. These are the seams that make the product demoable to a prospect and shape its architecture for tenants.

The technical core debi depends on is a serializable manifest. The V1 dashboards carry hand-written manifests with in-code closures — KPI and table-column formatters — that a stored, machine-generated dashboard cannot serialize; debi therefore drives formatting from tokens and declarative rules, so a generated template round-trips as plain data, and the same seam lets the app validate every dashboard debi proposes — against both the chart schema and the user's real columns — before it ever renders. Alongside debi, the V1 column→field mapping evolves from a dropdown editor into a three-panel drag-and-drop schema-assignment surface, with the keyboard/dropdown editor kept as the accessible fallback.

Private templates are the first per-user-private data in d3bi, and they open the security ladder the product starts climbing here: rather than pull row-level security in early, they are scoped at the application layer — an owner column plus reads filtered by the authenticated user — with database-enforced isolation deferred to V3 and each rung designed toward SOC 2. The work is in development now: the app shell and the two-skin seam are built, with the gallery, the drag-and-drop surface, debi itself, and the marketing landing scaffolded as wired stubs behind the nav, their bodies following as wireframes and a brand sheet arrive.

objectives.body: debi takes a request in plain language, reads what the user's data actually supports through the readiness loop, and emits a full dashboard — panels, KPIs, layout — that renders live and saves as a reusable private template. It never fabricates a metric, because every number it shows traces to the validated earned-value engine rather than to model prose.

The defining technical requirement of debi: it must emit a serializable manifest — formatting expressed as tokens and declarative rules — rather than the in-code closures the hand-written V1 manifests carry, so a generated dashboard round-trips as plain data and can be validated against the chart schema and the user's real columns before it renders.

objectives.lead: Reframe into a multi-tenant-ready product workspace
objectives.body: A public request-a-demo front door, a multi-template gallery (a second prebuilt template — aviation — joins transit) that presents the product as a multi-project workspace, a program/project switcher, and the first per-user-private data: the seams that make the product demoable to prospects and shape the architecture for tenants. Full database-enforced isolation is the V3 step; this version lays its foundation, with each security rung designed toward SOC 2.

Evolve the V1 column→field mapping from a dropdown editor into a three-panel drag-and-drop surface where a user drags their own columns onto canonical fields with type-compatibility enforced, while keeping the keyboard/dropdown editor as the accessible fallback.
Introduce a distinct site brand for the new chrome while leaving the proven dashboard visual system untouched — one product, two coordinated skins driven from one token seam.

challenges.body: The hand-written manifests carry closures (KPI and table-column formatters), which a stored, machine-generated dashboard cannot serialize. debi therefore drives formatting from tokens and declarative rules, so a generated template round-trips as plain data — and the same seam that makes the manifest serializable is what lets the app validate every dashboard debi proposes, against both the chart schema and the user's real columns, before it ever renders.

challenges.lead: Generative AI carries a per-use cost
challenges.body: Every dashboard debi builds is several model round-trips, and that inference is billed per token — a real, recurring, per-user cost the V1 templates never had. Immediate mitigations hold it down: the static knowledge debi relies on (the chart, metric, and dataset catalogs) is prompt-cached and shared across users, so it is near-free after the first call; trivial requests route to a smaller model; iterations are capped; and usage is metered per user. The structural fix arrives in V3 — an MCP server and CLI that let customers run debi on their own Claude subscription, moving the inference cost to them.

challenges.lead: Drag-and-drop on a schema that doesn't store types
challenges.body: The captured source columns carry no datatype, so type-compatible drops need either inference at assignment time (the first cut, no migration) or capture at ingest (a migration). The fix reuses the existing mapping-save endpoint, adds server-side type validation, builds the surface on a mature drag-and-drop toolkit, and keeps the dropdown editor as the accessible path.

The new site brand must not disturb the shipped dashboard visuals. A two-skin seam resolves it: the shell carries data-surface="shell" and reads --shell-* tokens that, for now, alias the existing dashboard tokens; when the brand sheet lands, those tokens are redefined under a brand selector to re-skin the chrome while the dashboard boards keep reading their original tokens.

challenges.lead: Redistributing the chrome without a rewrite
challenges.body: The single dashboard header is split into three zones (site top bar, left nav, slim per-dashboard header), with readiness computed once and shared so the in-body summary and the header pill never drift. A related move: the "best on desktop" banner lives in the root layout today and must shift down into the app shell once the root becomes the fully responsive public landing.

challenges.lead: Per-user-private data on the path to multi-tenant isolation
challenges.body: Private templates are the first per-user-private data and nudge the boundary V3 will formalize. Rather than pull row-level security in early, they are scoped at the application layer — an owner column plus reads filtered by the authenticated user — with the database-enforced, SOC 2-aligned isolation deferred to V3 and the SaaS release, and the decision logged as an ADR at build.

futureFeatures.lead: Wireframes and a brand sheet drive the per-screen build
futureFeatures.body: The visual skin and final layouts are gated on incoming wireframes and a brand sheet; once in, each screen is packaged for design, then surfaces B–E are built on the shell that exists today.

Project (a flat rename) versus program-contains-contracts (two-level, truer to the domain — East Link is the program, E130/E320 are contracts within it). The plan is to wireframe the two-level seam and ship flat first.

futureFeatures.lead: Take debi's cost off d3bi — an MCP server and a CLI
futureFeatures.body: debi's dashboard-building tools are exposed as an MCP server, so a customer connects their own Claude (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a claude.ai connector) and their subscription pays for the inference — debi then costs d3bi only the hosting and the database. A CLI brings the same tools to scripted and local workflows. Both run on the exact tool layer the in-app debi already uses, so the MCP server and CLI are additional front doors onto one backend, not a second system: a metered, branded in-app assistant for everyone, and a bring-your-own-Claude path for power users with no per-token bill to d3bi.

futureFeatures.lead: The security and compliance ladder, toward SOC 2
futureFeatures.body: Beyond today's authentication gate and the application-layer scoping introduced here, the roadmap is row-level security plus audit logging for true multi-user, then multi-tenant isolation for the SaaS — each rung built to satisfy SOC 2, which is the named compliance target for that work.

futureFeatures.lead: From demo surface to live tenants
futureFeatures.body: The request-a-demo flow, the multi-template gallery, and the program/project switcher are the multi-tenant demo seams now; database-enforced per-tenant isolation — each customer's data fenced at the database — is the SaaS step that turns the demo into real tenancy.

title: d3bi.app — Custom MCP and CLI (V3.0)
blurb: A custom MCP server and CLI that let a customer drive debi from their own Claude subscription — connect Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a claude.ai connector and their subscription pays for the inference, so debi costs d3bi only hosting and the database. Both run on the exact tool layer the in-app debi already uses — additional front doors onto one backend, not a second system. The same phase pairs a zero-token direct-manipulation build/edit mode, promotes security to database-enforced row-level security and audit logging (the SOC 2 layer above V2's application-layer scoping), and opens a controlled early access: six-month trials for up to five customers with usage metering and quotas live.
label: CAPSTONE
detail: V3 takes d3bi from an impressive demo to something a handful of real customers can run on their own data, and makes debi sustainable at that scale. The headline is a custom MCP server and a CLI: a customer connects their own Claude (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a claude.ai connector) and drives debi on their own subscription, moving inference cost off d3bi — the MCP server and CLI are additional front doors onto the exact tool backend in-app debi already uses, not a second system. Three pillars round it out: a secondary, direct-manipulation build/edit mode for fast, zero-token changes; the SOC 2 security layer (database-enforced row-level security and audit logging, above V2's application-layer scoping); and a controlled release — six-month trials for up to five customers with usage metering and quotas live.
description:
V3 takes d3bi from an impressive demo to something a small set of real customers can run on their own data — and makes debi sustainable at that scale. Its headline is a custom MCP server and a CLI. Every dashboard debi builds is several model round-trips billed per token — a real, recurring, per-user cost the V1 templates never had. The MCP server exposes debi's dashboard-building tools to a customer's own Claude (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or a claude.ai connector), so their subscription pays for the inference and debi costs d3bi only hosting and the database; the CLI brings the same tools to scripted and local workflows. Both run on the exact tool layer the in-app debi already uses, so they are additional front doors onto one backend rather than a second system — a metered, branded in-app assistant for everyone, and a bring-your-own-Claude path for power users with no per-token bill to d3bi.

Alongside the bring-your-own-Claude path, V3 adds a second way to author. debi (conversational, generative) and a direct-manipulation editor (double-click to rename, right-click to recolor, drag to arrange — no model call) become two front doors onto the same serializable manifest: debi for the generative path, the direct editor for fast, no-cost edits, and either able to open and change what the other produced. Neither is a separate dashboard format, so a board authored by conversation can be hand-edited and a hand-built board handed back to debi.

Security is promoted from the application to the database. The per-user ownership introduced in V2 — an owner column plus reads filtered by the authenticated user — becomes database-enforced row-level security plus audit logging, the SOC 2 rungs that make per-user (and, next, per-tenant) isolation a property of the database rather than an assertion the application makes. Row-level security is added beneath the existing owner-column filter, which was deliberately written to match the future database predicate, so the application keeps working unchanged while the database starts enforcing what it already asserted; a new authenticated surface, the MCP server, carries the same auth and ownership scoping with request logging and rate limiting, and its data flows are recorded in subprocessor and data-flow documentation. These SOC 2-aligned controls land before the first trial tenant's data does, not after.

On top of that foundation, V3 runs a controlled early access: up to five customers onboarded on their own data for six months, with live metering, quotas, paid-overage hooks, a feedback loop, and the support and incident handling a real customer relationship requires. Where V2 proved debi could author a dashboard from a sentence, V3 proves d3bi can put that in front of paying-track customers without the inference bill, the isolation gap, or manual onboarding becoming the limiting factor.

objectives.lead: Move inference cost off the critical path with an MCP server and CLI
objectives.body: The MCP server exposes debi's tools to a customer's own Claude; the CLI brings them to scripted and local workflows. For any customer on the bring-your-own-Claude path, d3bi pays for hosting and the database, not per-token inference — the same tool backend, billed to whoever holds the Claude subscription.

objectives.lead: Two authoring modes, one source of truth
objectives.body: debi (conversational, generative) and a direct-manipulation editor (double-click to rename, right-click to recolor, drag to arrange — no model call) are both front doors onto the same serializable-manifest backend: debi for the generative path, the direct editor for fast, no-cost edits, and either able to open and change what the other produced.

The application-layer ownership introduced in V2 becomes database-enforced row-level security plus audit logging — the SOC 2 rungs that make per-user (and, next, per-tenant) isolation a property of the database, not just an assertion the application makes.
Onboard up to five customers on their own data for six months: live metering, quotas, paid-overage hooks, a feedback loop, and the support and incident handling a real customer relationship requires.

Row-level security is added beneath the existing owner-column filter, which was deliberately written to match the future database predicate; the application keeps working unchanged while the database starts enforcing what the application already asserted. Decision logged as an ADR at build.

challenges.body: The MCP server carries the same authentication and per-user ownership scoping as the app, with request logging and rate limiting; data egresses under the customer's own Claude account and is recorded in the subprocessor/data-flow documentation.

challenges.lead: Real customer data raises the compliance bar
challenges.body: The SOC 2-aligned controls — row-level security, audit logging, metering, retention, and the documented data flows — land before the first trial tenant's data does, not after.

futureFeatures.body: Each customer fenced at the database — the SaaS step that turns five hand-picked trials into open tenancy.
Convert trials to paid without hand-onboarding; activation-gated signup becomes open signup.
User-defined measures first, then a composable chart grammar so debi can compose novel visuals — not only the prebuilt vocabulary — while every output stays validated against the data and on-brand.
Type I, then Type II, assessed against the controls this phase builds — the compliance program as the named outcome of the security ladder.
